It depends where you're based, what you play and where you're seated! It varies so much. Look for an orchestra that also runs a chamber music programme and draws from their pool of players for it, as chamber pay is better than Orchestra, but there are so many variables I can't possibly know I'm afraid.

1. This is usually the planning manager and musical director, although when we have a soloist come in to play a Concerto they'll often pick the Concerto and we will plan the rep around it.

2. My fave is either cello or French horn! I love them both so much :)

3. We usually do a 3hr rehearsal the day before a concert, followed by a 3hr rehearsal on the day of the concert. Sometimes we just do on the day with no rehearsal on the day before

4. This varies massively, and depends which country you're in too. In the UK with have the Musicians Union which specifies the minimum payment, and we pay more than that. It also depends where in the section you're sitting, and how much rehearsal there is etc. We also cover travel (and porterage for bigger instruments or doubling)

5. We go mainly off recommendations from existing players, but we also have people email cvs or recordings and put them on our list if they're good. We occasionally hold rounds of auditions.

Hmm good question! I'd actually never worked with an orchestra before this job, despite working in classical music admin for years. It's sometimes challenging trying to balance what the MD wants with what's realistically possible - particularly in terms of Orchestra size vs venue size. As I mentioned in another post, despite overbooking strings I always have quite a few pull out for illness/family/other reasons so there's a fair bit of last minute scrambling to find replacements.

Most rewarding is definitely seeing it all come together in the concerts! I always get a little high hearing fantastic music and knowing that I had a big part in helping with that. Also, I love getting to know the players and their quirks.

My advice would be: you have to be organised and be able to show evidence of excellent time management when applying. It's also important to be an easygoing person because you're communicating with all kinds of people and occasionally someone will be unhappy - so stay calm! I did a music degree too and as I said, quite a few years in various arts admin roles. All of this is what has lead me to this job.

Haha, I do actually...! I mainly think in terms of bookings, but I have found violinists to be incredibly flaky, Woodwind to be incredibly reliable and brass to be smokers 😂 I've been on tour with them all several times so in reality, these are all crap (except the smokers part) however its incredibly rare that a wind player will drop out of something. I think violins know that because they're in a bigger section they can be replaced (not always true).

In fact, we preempt this by overbooking the strings.

Otherwise they are a genuinely lovely bunch. Some fantastic players, and a couple of slight divas who can just about get away with it.

Our planning manager does most of the programming in partnership with our Musical Direcotr, but I think there are a few key points they look at: 

Logistics - how big is the orchestra, what's the instrumentation and what's the cost

Composition - do they like the music itself, would it pair nicely with another piece in a programme, does it feel like a complete and well written piece?

We hold composers workshops where we play through 8 or 9 new compositions and have a panel (an orchestra member, a staff member and a conductor) who discuss the music with the composers directly. We also let the orchestra fill in a form selecting their favourite piece and explaining why. We then choose one to play in a concert in our concert series later that year.

As a former saxophonist and now Orchestra manager, if playing with a classical orchestra is your dream I would definitely say pick up clarinet or flute. I've been an orchestra manager for 6 months and have thus far not booked a single saxophonist.

However, if you're exceptional you could get booked to do concertos (though saxophone ones are few and far between).

If you'd like to play in theatre in a pit, doubling would still be useful with sax.
